why: A bitmask as a set: keep the set of letters seen an odd number of times as a 26-bit mask, toggled with XOR at each character. A substring has all-even counts exactly when the masks at its two ends are equal, so the answer is the widest gap between two equal masks: remember each mask's first index in a hash map.
hints: A letter occurs an even number of times in S[l..r] when its count before l and its count up to r have the same parity.
Keep one parity bit per letter: a 26-bit mask updated with XOR as you scan. Equal masks at two positions mean the substring between them is all-even.
Store the first index where each mask appears (mask 0 at index -1) and take the longest i - first[mask]. O(N) time, at most 2^26 but really at most N+1 masks.
pitfalls: Forgetting the empty prefix (mask 0 at index -1), which is needed when the whole prefix is the answer, as in "zthtzh".
Overwriting the first index with later ones: keep the earliest index to get the longest span.
Returning 1 for no answer: a non-empty all-even substring has even length, so the answer is 0 when none exists.
statement:
You are given a string S of N lowercase English letters. Return the length of the longest substring (a contiguous segment) in which every letter occurs an even number of times. If no non-empty substring qualifies, return 0.

Worked example. S = "bdaaadadb":

  • "aa" (length 2) and "adad" (length 4) qualify.
  • "aaadad" (positions 2 to 7) has a = 4 and d = 2, both even: length 6.
  • No longer substring qualifies: the whole string has two bs and four as, but three ds, which is odd.

Answer: 6. For "abacb" the answer is 0; for "zthtzh" the whole string qualifies, so the answer is 6.
constraints:
• 1 <= N <= 100,000
  • S consists only of lowercase letters 'a'-'z'
  • An O(N) or O(N · 26) solution is expected.
